originalTitle: Trump promised a 'golden age' for agriculture. Farmers in Iowa say they're still waiting
summary: President Donald Trump has promised a "golden age" for agriculture, but farmers in Iowa and elsewhere are struggling with tariffs and the Iran war.
content:
IOWA — Farmer Aaron Lehman's health insurance premiums have more than doubled since the start of the year, after Congress decided not to extend federal subsidies after they ended. As the Iran war drags on, the cost of diesel , fertilizer and other inputs he relies on to run his Polk City farm are up. And crop prices have been concerningly low .

Lehman grows soybeans, corn, oats and hay on the land his family has worked for five generations. The Lehmans and other Iowa farmers have endured difficult times, but 2026 — with all the volatility around trade and foreign wars — feels different from recent years, Lehman said, despite President Donald Trump 's promises of a " golden age of American agriculture ."

"Farmers are really tightening their belts," Lehman, president of the Iowa Farmers Union , a nonpartisan organization that works to advance the causes of farmers and sustainable agriculture, told CNBC on his farm.

"It's one thing to say there's a golden age of agriculture right around the corner. Where?" Lehman said. "There's no indication that we're progressing towards healthier family farmers, that our rural communities are thriving under these policies."

Lehman is one of many farmers — normally a reliably conservative group — voicing his concerns about the administration's policies and raising alarms about the direction of the agricultural economy in Iowa, as well as throughout much of the country.

The White House, in a statement to CNBC, pinned the blame on Trump's predecessor.

"Farmers suffered for years under Joe Biden , who increased the United States' trade deficit to over $1.2 trillion, raised input costs, and pushed woke DEI agricultural policies," White House spokesperson Anna Kelly said.

In addition to criticizing the Biden administration for not securing trade deals, which Trump said crippled the agricultural sector, the president has touted his rollbacks of certain regulations and the doubling of the so-called "death tax" exemption , which eases the financial burden on heirs when farmers pass down their equipment and acreage.

Trump also ordered his administration to distribute $12 billion in direct payments to farmers using tariff revenue. In late June, the White House sent an $87.6 billion supplemental funding request to Congress mostly to help pay for the Iran war but also including more than $10 billion in aid to farmers. The House in July approved a $95 billion budget package to help fund the war that includes $12 billion in farm aid.

But his tariff regime has shut off markets that U.S. farmers rely on heavily. The Iran war has put pressure on supply for necessities such as fuel and fertilizer and has at times sent prices soaring. And inflation and high healthcare costs have only increased the pressure on farmers.

Amid these headwinds, approval of Trump has fallen to new lows among rural voters, according to a Fox News poll released in July. That poll found just 44 percent of rural Americans approve of Trump, down 14 points from the same poll taken in June.

That's higher than Trump's 40% approval rating among voters across the country, according to the CNBC All-America Economic Survey, released July 17, but down from 60% approval among rural voters at the start of his second term. It's a potentially troubling development for Republicans ahead of the 2026 midterms , in which they're trying to stave off a Democratic wave and retain narrow majorities in the U.S. House and Senate.

At best, Trump's impact on farmers has been a mixed bag, according to Chad Hart , an economics professor at Iowa State University.

Hart said the farm economy was already struggling at the beginning of the second Trump administration but that things have gotten worse and less predictable.

"I think farmers felt they had their pathway forward," Hart said, of the period at the start of Trump's latest term. "Change in policies meant we've seen more uncertainty there, and I think that has led to more concern for farmers as they're looking forward. Because right now they're not necessarily seeing where the endpoint is going to be with a lot of this."

Figures published by the American Farm Bureau Federation in July paint a bleak picture.

High inflation, low commodity prices and volatile production costs are projected to lead to a $32 billion loss on major crops in 2027 for U.S. farmers, up from a $31 billion projected loss in 2026, the trade group reported.

In an April survey , the group found 70% of U.S. farmers said they couldn't afford all the fertilizer they need.

Meanwhile, a joint report published this month by Iowa State University, the Iowa Farm Bureau and the Iowa Bankers Association found farm bankruptcies were up in 2025 and 2026 over those of the previous several years, both in Iowa and nationwide. The groups also reported that 19% of midsize and large Iowa farms they sampled were financially vulnerable in December 2025, more than double the number in 2022.

And more than a quarter of farmers, ranchers and agricultural managers rely on individual market health insurance, which is mainly composed of Affordable Care Act plans, according to an analysis by the Kaiser Family Foundation . That means many, such as Lehman, could be facing higher premiums since the ACA subsidies expired in January, as most congressional Republicans refused to extend them.

Marc Short , who was White House director of legislative affairs in Trump's first term in office, wrote in a recent Washington Post op-ed that "President Trump's trade policies have punched farmers in the mouth."

Trump's tariffs on China, which led to retaliatory duties and a Chinese pivot to other markets for products such as soybeans, have been particularly damaging, Short said in an interview with CNBC.

chineseTitle: 特朗普承诺农业将迎来“黄金时代”。爱荷华州的农民表示他们仍在等待
chineseSummary: 唐纳德·特朗普总统承诺农业的“黄金时代”，但爱荷华州和其他地方的农民正在与关税和伊朗战争作斗争。
chineseContent:
爱荷华州——国会决定在联邦补贴结束后不再延长联邦补贴，自今年年初以来，农民亚伦·雷曼(Aaron Lehman)的健康保险费增加了一倍多。随着伊朗战争的拖延，他赖以经营波尔克城农场的柴油、化肥和其他投入品的成本不断上涨。农作物价格一直低得令人担忧。

雷曼家族在其家族五代人耕种的土地上种植大豆、玉米、燕麦和干草。雷曼兄弟和爱荷华州的其他农民经历了困难时期，但雷曼表示，尽管唐纳德·特朗普总统承诺将迎来“美国农业的黄金时代”，但由于贸易和对外战争的种种波动，2026 年感觉与近年来有所不同。

“农民们确实在勒紧裤腰带，”爱荷华州农民联盟主席雷曼在他的农场告诉 CNBC。爱荷华州农民联盟是一个致力于推进农民事业和可持续农业事业的无党派组织。

“说农业的黄金时代即将到来是一回事。在哪里？”雷曼说。 “没有迹象表明我们正在向更健康的家庭农民迈进，我们的农村社区在这些政策下正在蓬勃发展。”

雷曼是众多农民中的一员——通常是可靠的保守派群体——表达了他对政府政策的担忧，并对爱荷华州以及全国大部分地区的农业经济方向发出了警报。

白宫在给 CNBC 的一份声明中将责任归咎于特朗普的前任。

白宫发言人安娜·凯利说：“乔·拜登领导下的农民多年来遭受苦难，他将美国的贸易逆差增加到超过 1.2 万亿美元，提高了投入成本，并推行了唤醒 DEI 农业政策。”

除了批评拜登政府没有达成贸易协议（特朗普称这削弱了农业部门）之外，总统还大肆宣扬他取消了某些法规，并将所谓的“死亡税”豁免加倍，这减轻了农民传承设备和土地时继承人的经济负担。

特朗普还命令他的政府利用关税收入向农民直接支付 120 亿美元。 6月底，白宫向国会提出了876亿美元的补充资金请求，主要用于帮助支付伊朗战争费用，但也包括超过100亿美元的对农民的援助。众议院 7 月批准了一项 950 亿美元的预算方案，为战争提供资金，其中包括 120 亿美元的农业援助。

但他的关税制度关闭了美国农民严重依赖的市场。伊朗战争给燃料和化肥等必需品的供应带来压力，有时导致价格飙升。通货膨胀和高昂的医疗费用只会增加农民的压力。

福克斯新闻 7 月份发布的一项民意调查显示，在这些不利因素的影响下，农村选民对特朗普的支持率已降至新低。该民意调查发现，只有 44% 的美国农村地区支持特朗普，比 6 月份的同一项民意调查下降了 14 个百分点。

根据 7 月 17 日发布的 CNBC 全美经济调查，这高于特朗普在全国选民中 40% 的支持率，但低于他第二任期开始时农村选民中 60% 的支持率。对于 2026 年中期选举之前的共和党人来说，这可能是一个令人不安的事态发展，他们正试图在中期选举中阻止民主党浪潮，并在美国众议院和参议院保持微弱多数。

爱荷华州立大学经济学教授查德·哈特表示，特朗普对农民的影响充其量是好坏参半。

哈特表示，在特朗普第二届政府执政之初，农业经济已经陷入困境，但情况变得更糟且更难以预测。

“我认为农民们觉得他们已经找到了前进的道路，”哈特在谈到特朗普最新任期开始时说道。 “政策的变化意味着我们看到了更多的不确定性，我认为这让农民在展望未来时更加担忧。因为现在他们不一定能看到很多事情的终点在哪里。”

美国农业局联合会七月份公布的数据描绘了一幅黯淡的景象。

该贸易组织报告称，高通胀、低商品价格和不稳定的生产成本预计将导致 2027 年美国农民主要农作物损失 320 亿美元，高于 2026 年预计的 310 亿美元损失。

在四月份的一项调查中，该组织发现 70% 的美国农民表示他们买不起所需的全部化肥。

与此同时，爱荷华州立大学、爱荷华州农业局和爱荷华州银行家协会本月发布的一份联合报告发现，2025 年和 2026 年爱荷华州和全国范围内的农场破产数量比前几年有所增加。这些组织还报告称，到 2025 年 12 月，他们抽样的爱荷华州中型和大型农场中有 19% 面临财务脆弱，这一数字是 2022 年的两倍多。

根据凯撒家庭基金会的分析，超过四分之一的农民、牧场主和农业管理者依赖个人市场健康保险，该保险主要由平价医疗法案计划组成。这意味着，自 ACA 补贴于 1 月份到期以来，雷曼兄弟等许多公司可能面临更高的保费，因为大多数国会共和党人拒绝延长补贴。

特朗普第一任期内担任白宫立法事务主任的马克·肖特(Marc Short)在《华盛顿邮报》最近的一篇专栏文章中写道，“特朗普总统的贸易政策打了农民的嘴”。

肖特在接受 CNBC 采访时表示，特朗普对中国征收的关税造成了特别大的损害，这导致了报复性关税以及中国将产品转向大豆等其他市场。

“在第一届政府中，我们还评估了对中国的关税，这对农民产生了影响。但我认为有一种说法解释了为什么中国是我们国家最大的威胁，”副总统肖特说。
